parts.title: The History of Cryptography
parts.text:
The practice of concealing the meaning of a message from anyone other than its intended recipient is almost as old as written language itself, with evidence of deliberate encryption techniques appearing across numerous ancient civilisations long before the development of any formal mathematical theory to support them. One of the earliest documented examples is the Caesar cipher, reportedly used by Julius Caesar to protect military communications, in which each letter of the original message is simply shifted a fixed number of places through the alphabet, a method so straightforward by modern standards that it can be broken almost instantly using basic computational tools, yet one that would have proven genuinely effective against the vast majority of people in the ancient world who could not read at all, let alone attempt to decode a disguised message. Ancient Egyptian scribes and Spartan military commanders, using a device known as a scytale to encode messages on a wrapped strip of leather, independently developed their own comparably rudimentary methods around the same broad historical period, suggesting the basic impulse to conceal written communication arose repeatedly across unconnected cultures.

For many centuries following these early efforts, cryptography remained a largely ad hoc craft practised by individual scholars, diplomats and military officers, with little systematic theoretical foundation underlying the various methods in use. A significant conceptual advance arrived during the Islamic Golden Age, when scholars such as Al-Kindi developed the technique of frequency analysis, a method for breaking substitution ciphers by examining how often particular letters or symbols appeared within an encrypted message and comparing these frequencies against the known statistical patterns of ordinary written language. This breakthrough effectively rendered simple substitution ciphers insecure for anyone aware of the technique, driving a centuries-long arms race between those devising increasingly elaborate methods of encryption, such as the polyalphabetic ciphers that emerged in Renaissance Europe specifically to resist frequency analysis, and those developing correspondingly sophisticated methods of codebreaking in response.

The twentieth century witnessed a dramatic transformation in both the sophistication and strategic importance of cryptography, driven substantially by the demands of global warfare. The German Enigma machine, used extensively during the Second World War to encrypt military communications, employed a complex system of rotating mechanical wheels to produce a cipher that its designers believed to be effectively unbreakable, generating an almost incomprehensibly vast number of possible letter combinations for any given message. The Allied codebreaking effort centred at Bletchley Park in England, which notably included the mathematician Alan Turing among its personnel, eventually succeeded in systematically breaking the Enigma cipher using early electromechanical computing devices specifically built for the purpose, an achievement widely credited with shortening the war considerably and one that simultaneously laid essential groundwork for the subsequent development of modern electronic computing, though the full details of the Bletchley Park effort remained officially classified for several decades after the war's conclusion.

The advent of digital computing and, subsequently, the internet, fundamentally transformed cryptography once again, shifting the field's central challenge from securing a handful of military communications to protecting the vast and continuous flow of digital data generated by billions of ordinary users worldwide. The development of public-key cryptography during the 1970s represented a particularly revolutionary conceptual breakthrough, enabling two parties who had never previously met or exchanged any secret information to nonetheless communicate securely over an inherently insecure and openly monitored channel, a seemingly paradoxical capability achieved through ingenious underlying mathematics involving numbers that are computationally trivial to multiply together but extraordinarily difficult to factor back into their original components. This mathematical asymmetry, combined with steadily increasing key lengths as computing power grew, has allowed public-key systems to remain broadly secure against conventional computing attacks for several decades since their introduction.

Modern cryptography now underpins an enormous range of everyday digital activities that most users never consciously think about, from securing online banking transactions and protecting private messaging applications to authenticating software updates and safeguarding government communications. Looking toward the future, researchers are increasingly focused on developing so-called post-quantum cryptography, encryption methods specifically designed to remain secure even against the vastly greater computational power that fully realised quantum computers are expected to eventually bring to bear against many of the mathematical problems underlying today's most widely used encryption standards, a looming challenge that cryptographers worldwide are racing to adequately prepare for well before such machines become a genuine practical threat, with several national standards agencies having already begun formally evaluating and selecting candidate post-quantum algorithms for future widespread adoption.

parts.title: The Gut Microbiome and Human Health
parts.text:
The human gut is home to an estimated trillions of microorganisms, collectively referred to as the gut microbiome, comprising bacteria, viruses, fungi and other microbes whose combined genetic material vastly exceeds that of the human genome itself. Once regarded chiefly as passive inhabitants with little relevance to overall health beyond their role in digestion, these microbial communities are now understood to participate actively in an extraordinarily wide range of physiological processes, prompting a fundamental reconsideration of the human body as a complex ecosystem rather than a self-contained biological unit operating in isolation.

Among the gut microbiome's most well-established functions is its central role in digesting food components that human digestive enzymes alone cannot break down, particularly complex dietary fibres found abundantly in plant-based foods. Through a process of bacterial fermentation, gut microbes convert these otherwise indigestible fibres into short-chain fatty acids, compounds that serve as an important energy source for the cells lining the colon and that have additionally been linked to reduced inflammation and improved metabolic regulation throughout the broader body, extending the microbiome's influence considerably beyond simple digestive function.

Perhaps the most unexpected area of gut microbiome research in recent years concerns its apparent influence on the brain and on mental health more broadly, a relationship researchers have termed the gut-brain axis. The vagus nerve, which runs directly between the gut and the brain, together with various chemical signalling molecules produced by gut bacteria, appears to establish genuine bidirectional communication between these two seemingly unrelated organ systems. Animal studies have demonstrated that deliberately altering gut bacterial composition can measurably affect anxiety-like behaviours and stress responses, while emerging human research has begun to identify associations, though not yet firmly established causal relationships, between specific patterns of gut microbial composition and conditions such as depression and anxiety disorders.

The composition of an individual's gut microbiome is shaped by a wide range of interacting factors, including diet, genetics, environmental exposures, specific medications, and critically, the particular circumstances surrounding early-life development. Infants delivered via caesarean section, for instance, tend to acquire a measurably different initial set of gut bacteria compared with those born vaginally, since vaginal birth exposes the infant directly to maternal microbes during the delivery process itself. Similarly, early use of antibiotics, while frequently medically necessary and often genuinely life-saving, can substantially disrupt the developing infant microbiome, with some researchers suggesting that such early disruptions may carry long-term consequences for immune system development and metabolic health later in life, though this remains an active and ongoing area of scientific investigation.

Diet represents one of the most significant and, importantly, one of the most readily modifiable factors influencing gut microbiome composition throughout adult life. Diets rich in diverse plant fibres have been consistently associated with greater microbial diversity, a characteristic generally regarded as a reliable marker of overall gut health, whereas diets high in processed foods and added sugars have instead been linked to reduced microbial diversity and to compositional shifts associated with increased inflammation throughout the body. This growing body of research has substantially fuelled considerable public and commercial interest in probiotic supplements and specifically formulated fermented foods, although the scientific evidence supporting many specific commercial probiotic health claims remains considerably more limited and preliminary than popular marketing materials frequently suggest to consumers, with the specific strains, dosages and health conditions tested in rigorous clinical trials often differing substantially from those actually present in products sold on supermarket shelves.

Despite the explosive recent growth in gut microbiome research and its accompanying wave of public enthusiasm, researchers caution that the field remains comparatively young, and that translating the substantial existing body of correlational findings into reliable, clinically actionable medical interventions will likely require considerably more time and rigorous further investigation. Nevertheless, the gut microbiome's demonstrated involvement in such a remarkably broad range of physiological processes, extending from basic digestion to immune regulation and even mental health, has firmly established it as one of the most genuinely promising and actively pursued frontiers in contemporary biomedical research. Several research teams are now pursuing personalised approaches that take an individual's unique existing microbiome composition into account when recommending dietary changes, though such personalised interventions remain largely experimental and are not yet widely available as standard, validated clinical practice.

YouTube is the most popular website in the world. It was created in 2005 by three former employees of an online payment company. At first, it was a simple [[website]] where people could upload and share short videos. Today, YouTube is used by more than two billion people every month. Users can watch almost anything on the platform, from music [[videos]] and film trailers to cooking lessons, video game streams, and news reports. Many people also use [[youtube]] to learn new skills, such as cooking, playing a musical instrument, or even speaking a foreign language.

For some people, YouTube has become more than just a hobby. Content creators, often called “YouTubers,” can earn money from advertisements shown before or during their videos. The most successful creators make millions of [[dollars]] a year and have audiences larger than many television channels.

In recent years, YouTube has continued to change the way people [[watch]] videos. Short, quick clips known as “Shorts” were introduced to compete with other popular apps, and they are now watched billions of times every day. The website also uses a powerful recommendation system that studies what each user watches and suggests similar videos, which keeps people watching for longer. As mobile phones have become more common, most people now watch YouTube on their [[phones]] rather than on a computer, showing just how much viewing habits have changed over time.

parts.title: India
parts.text:
## Paragraph I

The world's first university was established in India in 700 BC, where more than 10,500 students from around the world studied more than 60 different subjects. The training was conducted in Sanskrit. Nowadays, Sanskrit is considered to be the mother of all the European languages. Its elements can be traced in most of them.

## Paragraph II

The most frequently visited place in India is Delhi, the capital city of the country. It seems to be divided into two parts. New Delhi is a modern city with hi-tech architecture, tourist attractions and modern facilities. Old Delhi is several centuries old, with narrow streets, ancient churches and noisy bazaars. Lots of people live in slums without the most essential facilities like toilets and running water.

## Paragraph III

People all over the world know of India's greatest river, the Ganges. The river looks extremely beautiful in the morning light. It is the subject of thousands of prayers. It has become a common ritual for pilgrims to gather by the holy river in the mornings. It is believed that bathing in the Ganges helps to cure all kinds of diseases and can improve your life in general.

## Paragraph IV

Indian climate differs from one part of the country to another. The air is cool and fresh in the mountains, but in the plains it is usually very hot and dry, so even a short trip can be very hard for an inexperienced traveller. That is why tourists are always glad to have a rest at one of the numerous stations in the hills. There they can enjoy a nice cup of real Indian tea, the most refreshing drink in such a climate.

## Paragraph V

India is not all history. It is also famous for its Bollywood industry, which produces different films. Indian films have always had their own style; they are rich in music and dancing. Though the industry is still developing, many Indian film stars have received Oscar prizes and are known throughout the world. The home of Bollywood is Mumbai, also known as a busy port and the country's commercial centre.

## Paragraph VI

There is an unusual treasure hidden in the Indian mountains. These are striking ancient temples cut in the rocks. For example, the Buddhist cave temples at Ajanta were built at least 2,000 years ago. Inside the caves on the walls, tourists can see animal images and pictures of people's lives. Some researchers believe that the interpretation of the images can help us to learn a lot about people's lives in ancient times.

parts.title: The History of Paper Clips
parts.text:
Few everyday objects seem as unremarkable as the paper clip, yet its history is considerably more tangled than its simple appearance would suggest. Wire-based fasteners for holding sheets of paper together began to appear in patent offices across Europe and the United States during the final decades of the nineteenth century, as the growing volume of office correspondence created a genuine demand for a cheap, reusable alternative to pins and ribbon. Dozens of inventors registered variations on the theme, experimenting with loops, springs and clasps of every conceivable shape. The design that ultimately triumphed, now instantly recognisable as the double-loop ‘Gem’ clip, was never formally patented at all, and the identity of whoever first devised it remains, somewhat remarkably, a matter of historical uncertainty rather than settled record.

This gap in the historical record has, over the years, been filled by a persistent and widely repeated myth crediting the invention to a Norwegian inventor named Johan Vaaler, who patented a similar wire fastener in 1899. Closer examination of Vaaler's design, however, reveals a clip noticeably less practical than the Gem clip already being manufactured and sold in Britain and the United States at around the same time; his patent, moreover, appears to have had little if any commercial success. Historians now generally agree that Vaaler's contribution has been considerably overstated, yet the myth endures, buoyed in part by a sense of national pride and reinforced by the paper clip's later adoption as a patriotic symbol within Norway itself.

What makes the Gem clip's continued dominance particularly striking is the sheer number of attempts made to improve upon it. Since the early twentieth century, inventors have filed several hundred patents for alternative paper-fastening devices, many boasting supposedly superior grip, reduced tendency to snag or greater ease of use. Almost without exception, these alternatives have failed to displace the original design from stationery drawers around the world. Engineers who have studied the phenomenon point to an elegant balance between simplicity, cost and function: the double loop of wire distributes pressure evenly across a stack of paper, grips firmly without piercing the sheets, and can be manufactured from a single length of wire at negligible expense, a combination of virtues that later designs have found remarkably difficult to surpass.

Beyond its practical function, the paper clip has occasionally taken on a symbolic weight far exceeding its physical size. During the Second World War, when Nazi authorities occupying Norway banned the wearing of buttons bearing the image of the exiled King Haakon VII, some Norwegians reportedly began wearing paper clips on their lapels instead, adopting the humble object as a quiet, easily deniable gesture of national unity and resistance. Although historians have since questioned exactly how widespread this practice actually was, the story cemented the paper clip's association with Norwegian identity and resilience, an association that persists to this day, most visibly in the form of an enormous paper clip sculpture erected outside a factory in the country as a tribute to that wartime defiance.

In the decades since, the paper clip has continued to find uses that its original designers could scarcely have anticipated. Its slender wire has proved perfectly suited to tasks as varied as resetting an unresponsive electronic device, picking a simple padlock, or fashioning an improvised piece of jewellery. Despite the gradual shift toward digital documents and the corresponding decline in printed paperwork, the paper clip shows little sign of disappearing from desks and drawers, its usefulness seemingly undiminished by the passage of more than a century. Few inventions illustrate quite so vividly how an object of negligible cost and unassuming design can nonetheless secure a permanent, if largely unheralded, place in everyday life.

parts.title: Is Graffiti Art or Crime?
parts.text:
The term graffiti derives from the Italian graffito meaning ‘scratching’ and can be defined as uninvited marking or writing scratched or applied to objects, built structures and natural features. It is not a new phenomenon: examples can be found on ancient structures around the world, in some cases predating the Greeks and Romans. In such circumstances it has acquired invaluable historical and archaeological significance, providing a social history of life and events at that time. Graffiti is now a problem that has become pervasive, as a result of the availability of cheap and quick means of mark making. It is usually considered a priority to remove graffiti as quickly as possible after it appears. This is for several reasons. The first is to prevent ‘copy-cat’ emulation which can occur rapidly once a clean surface is defaced. It may also be of a racist or otherwise offensive nature and many companies and councils have a policy of removing this type of graffiti within an hour or two of it being reported. Also, as paints, glues and inks dry out over time they can become increasingly difficult to remove and are usually best dealt with as soon as possible after the incident. Graffiti can also lead to move serious forms of vandalism and, ultimately, the deterioration of an area, contributing to social decline.

Although graffiti may be regarded as an eyesore, any proposal to remove it from sensitive historic surfaces should be carefully considered: techniques designed for more robust or utilitarian surfaces may result in considerable damage. In the event of graffiti incidents, it is important that the owners of buildings or other structures and their consultants are aware of the approach they should take in dealing with the problem. The police should be informed as there may be other related attacks occurring locally. An incidence pattern can identify possible culprits, as can stylised signatures or nicknames, known as ‘tags’, which may already be familiar to local police. Photographs are useful to record graffiti incidents and may assist the police in bringing a prosecution. Such images are also required for insurance claims and can be helpful in cleaning operatives, allowing them to see the problem area before arriving on site.

There are a variety of methods that are used to remove graffiti. Broadly these divide between chemical and mechanical systems. Chemical preparations are based on dissolving the media; these solvents can range from water to potentially hazardous chemical ‘cocktails’. Mechanical systems such as wire-brushing and grit-blasting attempt to abrade or chip the media from the surface. Care should be taken to comply with health and safety legislation with regard to the protection of both passers-by and any person carrying out the cleaning. Operatives should follow product guidelines in terms of application and removal, and wear the appropriate protective equipment. Measures must be taken to ensure that run-off, aerial mists, drips and splashes do not threaten unprotected members of the public. When examining a graffiti incident it is important to assess the ability of the substrate to withstand the prescribed treatment. If there is any doubt regarding this, then small trial areas should be undertaken to assess the impact of more extensive treatment.

A variety of preventive strategies can be adopted to combat a recurring problem of graffiti at a given site. As no two sites are the same, no one set of protection measures will be suitable for all situations. Each site must be looked at individually. Surveillance systems such as closed-circuit television may also help. In cities and towns around the country, prominently placed cameras have been shown to reduce anti-social behavior of all types including graffiti. Security patrols will also act as a deterrent to prevent recurring attacks. However, the cost of this may be too high for most situations. Physical barriers such as a wall, railings, doors or gates can be introduced to discourage unauthorized access to a vulnerable site. However, consideration has to be given to the impact measures have on the structure being protected. In the worst cases, they can be almost as damaging to the quality of the environment as the graffiti they prevent. In others, they might simply provide a new surface for graffiti.

One of the most significant problems associated with graffiti removal is the need to remove it from surfaces that are repeatedly attacked. Under these circumstances, the repeated removal of graffiti using even the most gentle methods will ultimately cause damage to the surface material. There may be situations where the preventive strategies mentioned above do not work or are not a viable proposition at a given site. Anti-graffiti coatings are usually applied by brush or spray leaving a thin veneer that essentially serves to isolate the graffiti from the surface. Removal of graffiti from a surface that has been treated in this way is much easier, usually using low-pressure water which reduces the possibility of damage. Depending on the type of barrier selected it may be necessary to reapply the coating after each graffiti removal exercise.

parts.text:
Walking is one of the simplest forms of exercise, and it can be done almost anywhere. People do not need special equipment or a gym to go for a walk. A short [[Walk]] each day can help people stay active and improve their general health.

Walking can also be good for the mental [[health]]. Spending time outside may help reduce stress and improve a person's mood. Some people enjoy walking with friends because it gives them a chance to talk and spend [[time]] together.

Regular walking can have other benefits as well. It can make the heart stronger and help people maintain a healthy weight. Older [[people]] may also find that walking regularly helps them stay independent and move more easily.

Experts often recommend starting with short walks and slowly increasing the distance. The most important thing is to make walking a [[regular]] habit. Even a simple walk can become an important part of a healthy lifestyle. A person with sedentary [[lifestyle]] should change the habit and start walking to live longer.

Ideally it would be decorated in her favourite colours, and I'd need it ready to collect on Friday afternoon so there's time to set everything up before the party.

We've just moved into an older house, and I've already noticed the back door doesn't close properly and one of the garden fence panels is coming loose. Rather than paying a tradesperson for every small job, I'd like to buy some basic tools and get a bit of advice on how to tackle these repairs myself over the coming weekends.

Our dog has been rolling around in the garden all week and badly needs a proper wash and a trim before we drive up to visit relatives this weekend. While I'm there I'd also like to replace his old lead, which is starting to fray, and maybe pick up a few new toys to keep him occupied on the journey.

I'm getting married in just three weeks, and I've decided to wear my mother's old wedding dress rather than buy a new one. The only problem is that it's a little large around the waist and the sleeves are too long, so I need someone experienced who can take it in properly before the ceremony.

The heel came away from one of my work shoes this morning right as I was leaving the house, so I've been limping around all day in my spare pair. I also need a spare key cut for the office before lunchtime, since our receptionist keeps losing hers, so I'm hoping to sort both errands out in one visit.

My son has recently grown out of picture books and started enjoying much longer stories, but he's fairly particular about what interests him. I'd like to find somewhere quiet, away from a noisy high-street chain, where he can sit for a while, browse at his own pace and choose something for himself rather than me guessing what he'll like.

I'm hosting a dinner party at the weekend and have a rather long list of vegetables and salad ingredients to get through before Saturday evening. Rather than lugging several heavy bags home on the bus, I'd much prefer to have everything brought straight to my door, ideally from a supplier that sources locally rather than importing everything.

parts.title: Solar Panels
parts.text:
## Paragraph 15

Long before rooftop panels became a common sight, scientists were already curious about whether sunlight could be turned directly into electricity. In 1839, a French physicist noticed that certain materials produced a small electrical current when exposed to light, though nobody yet understood why this happened. It took more than a century of further study before researchers at an American laboratory built the first cell capable of powering a small device in the 1950s, marking the point at which the idea shifted from a laboratory curiosity into a technology with genuine practical potential.

## Paragraph 16

A solar panel is made up of many individual cells, most commonly built from silicon, a material that responds to light in a particular way. When sunlight strikes a cell, some of its energy is absorbed and knocks electrons loose from their usual positions within the material. Because the cell is constructed with layers that have slightly different properties, these freed electrons are pushed to flow in one direction rather than randomly, and it is this flow of electrons that we recognise as an electric current.

## Paragraph 17

Not every panel on the market is built in the same way. Some are made from a single, continuous crystal of silicon, which tends to convert sunlight into electricity more efficiently but costs more to produce. Others are formed from many smaller crystal fragments melted together; these are usually cheaper but slightly less efficient. A third option involves coating a surface with a very thin layer of light-absorbing material, which is lighter and more flexible than the other two but currently converts a smaller proportion of sunlight into usable power.

## Paragraph 18

Anyone thinking about fitting panels to their roof needs to consider more than simply the price of the equipment. The direction the roof faces and its angle both affect how much sunlight the panels will receive over the course of a year, and even partial shade from a nearby tree or chimney at certain times of day can noticeably reduce output. The roof itself must also be strong enough to bear the additional weight, and depending on where a person lives, permission from local authorities may be required before any work begins.

## Paragraph 19

The upfront cost of a solar installation can be substantial, which puts many households off before they look any further into it. Once that initial expense has been paid off, however, the ongoing running costs are extremely low, and in many regions the government offers grants or tax reductions to encourage households to switch. Some energy providers will also pay homeowners for any electricity their panels generate but don't use themselves, which is fed back into the wider network, gradually reducing the time it takes for the whole system to pay for itself.

## Paragraph 20

It would be easy to assume that solar panels are entirely beneficial for the planet, but the full picture is more complicated. Manufacturing the cells requires mining and processing raw materials, a process that itself consumes energy and can generate pollution. There is also the question of what happens to panels once they eventually wear out, since some of the materials inside them are difficult to recycle safely. Even so, most studies agree that the carbon emissions saved over a panel's working life far outweigh those created during its production and eventual disposal.

parts.title: The Māori People of New Zealand
parts.text:
According to oral tradition and archaeological evidence, the ancestors of today's Māori people arrived in what is now New Zealand from other parts of Polynesia in a series of ocean voyages, most likely completed by the late thirteenth century. Navigating open water in large ocean-going canoes known as waka, these early settlers relied on their knowledge of stars, ocean currents and bird movements rather than any instruments. Once ashore, they encountered a landscape unlike anything in their tropical homelands: noticeably colder temperatures, unfamiliar plants, and no land mammals beyond a few small species. Over the centuries that followed, the newcomers gradually adapted their farming methods, tools and diet to this new environment, and in doing so developed customs, beliefs and a language distinct enough from their wider Pacific relatives that a separate identity — Māori — had clearly emerged well before any European ships reached the islands.

Traditional Māori society was organised around kinship groups rather than a single unified nation. An iwi, often translated loosely as 'tribe', was made up of several smaller hapū, or sub-tribes, each tracing its descent from a shared ancestor through whakapapa, a genealogical record passed down orally across generations. At the heart of community life stood the marae, a communal courtyard with a carved meeting house where important gatherings, decisions, ceremonies and disputes were — and still are — addressed. Skilled carvers produced intricate wooden panels and canoes, while the practice of tā moko, permanent skin marking applied with traditional tools, conveyed a person's ancestry, achievements and standing at a glance. None of this was recorded in writing the way Europeans would later document history; instead, genealogy, mythology and tribal history were preserved through memorised chants, songs and storytelling, a system that demanded remarkable precision from those entrusted with it.

Te reo Māori, the Māori language, came under serious pressure following sustained European settlement in the nineteenth century. Schools actively discouraged its use, and by the middle of the twentieth century the proportion of Māori children who could speak it fluently had fallen sharply, prompting fears that the language might disappear within a generation or two. From the 1970s onward, however, a deliberate revival movement gathered pace. Community-run 'language nests', where pre-school children are immersed entirely in Māori from infancy, were established across the country, and te reo was granted official language status in 1987, putting it on equal legal footing with English. Dedicated broadcasters now produce television and radio content entirely in the language, and an annual Māori Language Week encourages the wider population to learn at least a handful of everyday words and phrases. While fluency rates remain far below those of the pre-colonial period, the long downward trend has clearly been reversed.

Sustained contact with European settlers began in earnest in the early nineteenth century and brought profound disruption. In 1840, representatives of the British Crown and a large number of Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, an agreement intended to establish a formal relationship between the two parties. Crucially, the Māori and English versions of the document did not say quite the same thing, particularly regarding how much authority chiefs were surrendering, and this discrepancy has fuelled disputes ever since. Within a few decades, disagreements over land and governance escalated into a series of armed conflicts, and vast areas of tribal land were subsequently confiscated or sold under circumstances many Māori considered unjust. The economic and social consequences of this loss of land proved long-lasting, contributing to disparities in wealth, health and education that persisted for generations afterward and that successive governments have only begun to seriously address in recent decades.

Since the 1970s, a formal body known as the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated historical breaches of the treaty and recommended compensation, including the return of land and significant financial settlements, to affected iwi. Māori representation in national politics has also grown, partly through a small number of parliamentary seats reserved specifically for Māori voters, and partly through wider participation in mainstream politics. Culturally, elements of Māori tradition have gained international recognition; the haka, a ceremonial chant and dance once performed before battle, is now closely associated with New Zealand's national rugby team and is performed at various public occasions around the world. Even so, considerable challenges remain: Māori communities continue to report, on average, worse outcomes in areas such as health, income and educational achievement than the population as a whole. Nevertheless, renewed pride in language, land and custom has left contemporary Māori identity considerably stronger than it was just a few decades ago.

parts.title: Galileo Galilei
parts.text:
Galileo Galilei was born in the Italian city of Pisa in 1564, the eldest son of a musician who hoped his son would pursue a respectable career in medicine. After enrolling at the University of Pisa to study exactly that, the young Galileo instead became captivated by mathematics, a subject he had encountered somewhat by accident through a tutor originally hired for a friend. He eventually left university without completing his medical degree, yet his growing reputation as a mathematician secured him a series of academic posts, first back at Pisa itself and later at the more prestigious University of Padua, where he would spend almost two decades developing both his teaching and his own private investigations into motion, mechanics and, eventually, the heavens above.

Galileo did not invent the telescope — that credit usually goes to a Dutch spectacle maker — but on hearing reports of the device in 1609, he set about building and steadily improving his own versions, eventually achieving a level of magnification far beyond anything else available in Europe at the time. Turning this improved instrument toward the night sky produced a series of discoveries that would unsettle long-held assumptions about the universe. He observed that the Moon's surface was pitted with craters and mountains rather than perfectly smooth, identified four small points of light orbiting Jupiter that could only be its moons, and later detected dark blemishes moving steadily across the face of the Sun. Each of these findings chipped away at the ancient philosophical idea that heavenly bodies were flawless and unchanging.

Perhaps the most consequential of Galileo's observations concerned the planet Venus, which he found to pass through a full cycle of phases much like the Moon does. Such a pattern could only be explained if Venus orbited the Sun rather than the Earth, lending strong observational support to a model proposed decades earlier by the astronomer Copernicus, in which the Sun, rather than the Earth, sat at the centre of the universe. Galileo became an outspoken defender of this heliocentric view, promoting it not only through specialist academic writing but in books composed in everyday Italian so that a much wider readership could follow his arguments. His most famous work on the subject, published in 1632, presented the debate as an extended conversation between three characters, a format that made his own position unmistakably clear despite its dialogue structure.

This growing public advocacy for heliocentrism eventually brought Galileo into direct conflict with the Catholic Church, which at the time endorsed the traditional view that the Earth remained motionless at the centre of creation. In 1616, church officials formally warned him against teaching the Copernican model as established fact, a restriction he appeared to respect for a number of years afterward. However, his 1632 publication was interpreted by many, including the Pope who had previously supported him, as breaching that earlier warning, and Galileo was summoned before the Inquisition the following year. After a lengthy trial, he was found guilty of what the Church termed a serious suspicion of heresy, forced to publicly renounce his views, and sentenced to spend the remainder of his life confined to his own home under close supervision.

Confinement did not end Galileo's scientific work, however. During his years under house arrest, going blind toward the very end of his life, he turned his attention back to the physics of motion, a subject he had studied much earlier in his career, and produced a treatise on mechanics that many historians regard as at least as important as his astronomical discoveries. He died in 1642, still formally condemned by the Church, and it was not until 1992 that the Vatican issued a statement acknowledging that the judgment against him had been mistaken. Today, Galileo is remembered as one of the central figures in the emergence of modern experimental science, valued as much for his insistence on testing ideas through careful observation as for any single discovery credited to his name.

His influence extended well beyond the specific facts he uncovered. By insisting that claims about the natural world be tested through measurement and experiment rather than settled purely by philosophical argument or appeal to ancient authority, Galileo helped establish a method of inquiry that later scientists across Europe would adopt and refine. Generations of astronomers built directly on his telescopic technique, while his mathematical treatment of falling bodies laid groundwork later developed further by Isaac Newton. For this combination of practical ingenuity and methodological rigour, many historians of science now consider him among the most influential figures of the entire scientific revolution.

Trees are an important part of our environment. They provide shade on hot days and make streets, parks, and gardens more pleasant. [[Trees]] also produce oxygen, which people and animals need to live.

Trees are also home to many animals. Birds build their nests in branches, while insects and other small [[animals]] live on or around trees. In forests, trees provide food and shelter for a large number of different species.

However, many [[forests]] are disappearing because people cut down trees for farming, buildings, and other purposes. Planting new trees is one way to protect the environment. parts.title: The Beauty Industry
parts.text:
## Paragraph 15

The use of cosmetics stretches back thousands of years, with archaeological evidence showing that ancient Egyptians applied kohl around their eyes as early as 4000 BC, partly for decoration and partly to protect against sun glare and infection. Ancient Chinese, Greek and Roman societies developed their own cosmetic traditions, using ingredients such as crushed minerals, plant extracts and even lead-based compounds, unaware at the time of the serious health risks some of these substances carried.

## Paragraph 16

Today, the beauty industry generates several hundred billion dollars in revenue annually across skincare, makeup, haircare and fragrance, making it one of the largest consumer sectors in the world. Growth has been especially rapid in emerging markets, where rising incomes and greater exposure to global media have introduced beauty routines once associated mainly with wealthier nations to a much broader customer base.

## Paragraph 17

Advertising within the beauty industry frequently promotes narrow and often unrealistic standards of appearance, and researchers have linked heavy exposure to such imagery with lower self-esteem and body dissatisfaction, particularly among young people. Social media has intensified this effect further, since heavily edited images circulate rapidly and are often difficult to distinguish from unaltered photographs, making unattainable standards appear ordinary and achievable.

## Paragraph 18

Because cosmetic products are applied directly to skin and, in many cases, absorbed into the body, governments in most countries require manufacturers to test formulations for safety before they reach store shelves. Regulatory bodies periodically update lists of banned or restricted ingredients as new scientific evidence about long-term health effects becomes available, and companies found violating these rules can face substantial fines or forced product recalls.

## Paragraph 19

The manufacturing and packaging of beauty products carries a significant environmental cost that has drawn growing criticism in recent years. Single-use plastic packaging, non-biodegradable ingredients such as certain synthetic microbeads, and the water and energy required for large-scale production all contribute to the industry's overall environmental footprint, prompting some brands to explore refillable containers and biodegradable formulations.

## Paragraph 20

In response to these concerns, a noticeable segment of the industry has begun shifting away from purely appearance-focused marketing toward messaging built around self-acceptance, inclusivity and ingredient transparency. Several major brands have introduced wider shade ranges, reduced digital retouching in their advertising, and published detailed ingredient lists, reflecting a broader cultural move toward valuing authenticity over an idealised, narrowly defined standard of beauty.

parts.title: The History of Spices
parts.text:
For thousands of years, spices have shaped trade, exploration and even the boundaries of empires. Long before refrigeration existed, dried spices such as pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg were prized not only for the flavour they added to food but also for their ability to preserve meat and mask the taste of ingredients that had begun to spoil. In the ancient world, spices travelled enormous distances along overland routes that connected South and Southeast Asia to the Mediterranean, passing through the hands of numerous merchants before reaching European markets. By the time a sack of pepper reached Rome or later Venice, its price had risen so dramatically that it was sometimes weighed out grain by grain and used almost like currency. In medieval Europe, pepper was so valuable that a labourer might need to work for several days simply to afford a small handful, and rents, dowries and fines were occasionally paid in peppercorns rather than coins.

For centuries, Arab and Venetian traders controlled the lucrative spice routes, and both groups guarded their sources with great secrecy. Arab merchants invented elaborate stories about the dangers of collecting cinnamon and pepper, describing fierce birds that guarded cinnamon groves or serpents that infested pepper forests, partly to discourage rivals from seeking the true origin of these goods. Venice, meanwhile, built its wealth and political power largely on its position as the gateway through which Eastern spices entered Europe, taxing every shipment that passed through its ports. This monopoly meant that ordinary Europeans paid extraordinary prices for spices that had cost very little at their original source, and it created enormous pressure among rival nations to find an alternative route to Asia.

Frustrated by Venetian and Arab control of the trade, European monarchs began funding voyages of exploration in search of a direct sea route to the spice-producing regions of Asia. In 1498, the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama became the first European to sail around Africa and reach India by sea, opening a route that bypassed the old overland monopolies entirely. A few years earlier, Christopher Columbus had set sail westward with the same goal of reaching Asia's spice markets, though he instead reached the Americas, an outcome nobody had anticipated. These voyages triggered what historians now call the Age of Exploration, as Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands and England competed fiercely to control spice-producing territories. The Portuguese crown quickly declared a royal monopoly over the pepper trade with India, and a single successful voyage could return profits large enough to fund an entire fleet the following year.

By the seventeenth century, the Dutch East India Company had emerged as the dominant force in the spice trade, particularly in the Moluccas, a group of islands in present-day Indonesia that were then the only known source of nutmeg and cloves. The company fought wars, formed alliances and sometimes committed brutal acts of violence to secure exclusive control over these islands. To keep prices high and eliminate competition, the Dutch deliberately destroyed nutmeg trees growing on islands outside their control, ensuring that the valuable spice could only be obtained through their own tightly regulated supply. Under the Treaty of Breda in 1667, the Dutch even traded the small island of Run, a nutmeg-producing territory, to England in exchange for a Dutch claim to Manhattan, illustrating just how highly nutmeg was valued at the time.

Today, spices are available cheaply and abundantly in supermarkets around the world, a striking contrast to their status centuries ago as luxury goods reserved for the wealthy. Modern transportation, large-scale cultivation and global trade networks have removed the scarcity that once made spices so valuable, though many dishes associated with historic spice routes remain popular worldwide. Spices continue to carry cultural significance in cuisines from India to Morocco to Mexico, often forming the backbone of national identity through food. In recent decades, growing interest in international cuisine has encouraged home cooks and professional chefs alike to experiment with spice combinations once confined to a single region, blending flavours from different culinary traditions in ways earlier generations could never have imagined. The history of spices serves as a reminder of how much of human exploration, conflict and cultural exchange has been driven by the pursuit of flavour.

parts.title: Propaganda
parts.text:
Propaganda is information, often biased or misleading, that is used to promote a particular political cause, ideology or point of view. Unlike straightforward advertising, which usually aims to sell a product, propaganda seeks to shape how people think, feel and behave on a much broader scale, frequently targeting entire populations rather than individual consumers. It can appear in many forms, including posters, films, speeches, news reports and, increasingly, social media content, and it is not always obviously false; effective propaganda frequently relies on selectively presenting true facts while omitting information that would complicate the intended message. Because it appeals to emotion rather than careful reasoning, propaganda can be remarkably persuasive even when the audience is aware that persuasion is taking place.

The term itself originates from the Catholic Church, which in 1622 established the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, or Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, an organisation created to spread Catholic teaching in territories where the Church wished to expand its influence. Although the word initially carried a fairly neutral meaning, simply referring to the spreading of ideas, it gradually acquired negative connotations during the twentieth century as governments around the world used propaganda on an unprecedented scale during wartime. Posters urging citizens to enlist, buy war bonds or conserve resources appeared throughout Europe and North America, demonstrating how propaganda could be mobilised to support a national cause during periods of crisis.

Propagandists rely on a recognisable set of techniques to influence their audience. Repetition is one of the most common, since ideas presented over and over tend to feel more familiar and, as a result, more trustworthy, even without supporting evidence. Another technique, sometimes called the use of glittering generalities, involves attaching a cause to vague but emotionally appealing words such as freedom, honour or progress, encouraging people to support an idea without examining it critically. Scapegoating, in which a particular group is blamed for social or economic problems, has also been used throughout history to unite a population against a common enemy, whether real or invented. The so-called bandwagon effect encourages individuals to adopt a belief simply because it appears that everyone else already holds it, exploiting the natural human desire to belong to a majority.

Totalitarian governments in the twentieth century developed some of the most extensive and systematic propaganda machinery in history. Regimes in Germany, the Soviet Union and elsewhere established dedicated ministries whose sole purpose was to control public information, censor dissenting opinions and produce material glorifying the state and its leadership. Newspapers, radio broadcasts, school textbooks and even children's games were adapted to reinforce official ideology, ensuring that citizens encountered consistent messaging from an early age throughout every aspect of daily life. Such thorough control over information made it extremely difficult for ordinary citizens to access alternative viewpoints or verify the accuracy of what they were being told, leaving many with little choice but to accept the official narrative.

In the twenty-first century, propaganda has adapted to new technology. Social media platforms allow messages to spread instantly to enormous audiences, and automated accounts, commonly called bots, can be used to amplify particular narratives, making a fringe opinion appear far more widespread than it truly is. Foreign governments and political groups have been accused of using targeted disinformation campaigns during elections, tailoring misleading content to specific demographic groups based on data collected from their online activity. Unlike traditional propaganda, which was often produced by an identifiable government agency, much of today's disinformation is difficult to trace back to its original source, which makes it considerably harder for the public to evaluate the credibility or motives behind the message they are viewing.

In response to these challenges, educators and journalists increasingly emphasise the importance of media literacy, the ability to critically evaluate the information a person encounters rather than accepting it automatically. Fact-checking organisations have emerged specifically to verify claims circulating online, tracing images, quotations and statistics back to their original context in order to expose manipulation. Some schools have introduced media literacy programmes designed to teach students how to identify emotionally manipulative language, recognise doctored images and question the motives behind a given piece of content before sharing it further. While these countermeasures cannot eliminate propaganda entirely, many experts argue that a well-informed and sceptical public remains one of the most effective defences against it.

parts.title: Online Dating
parts.text:
## Paragraph 15

Long before smartphones existed, computer-based matchmaking services attempted to pair individuals using questionnaires processed by early mainframe systems, an approach that seems primitive today but represented a genuine departure from the traditional methods of meeting a partner through family introductions, workplaces or chance encounters. The launch of dedicated websites in the 1990s allowed users to browse profiles from their own homes for the first time, gradually normalising the idea that a potential partner might be found through a screen rather than a shared social circle, though early adopters were often regarded with a degree of suspicion by those unfamiliar with the concept.

## Paragraph 16

Modern platforms rely on complex systems that analyse a user's stated preferences, browsing behaviour and even how long they linger on a particular profile, in order to surface matches judged statistically more likely to lead to mutual interest. Some services ask users to complete lengthy personality assessments before granting access, feeding the results into models originally developed by psychologists to study compatibility in long-term relationships, while others favour a simpler approach based largely on physical appearance and immediate reaction, reflecting sharply differing philosophies about what actually predicts a successful match.

## Paragraph 17

One of the most frequently cited advantages of meeting people this way is the sheer expansion of the pool of potential partners available to an individual, particularly for those living in smaller communities or working in isolating professions where chance encounters are rare. Users belonging to minority groups have also reported that these platforms make it considerably easier to find partners who share a particular identity, interest or background, a task that might otherwise depend heavily on luck within a limited local social circle.

## Paragraph 18

Despite its conveniences, this method of meeting people carries well-documented risks, chief among them the possibility that a person's profile bears little resemblance to who they actually are once met in person. Cases of individuals fabricating photographs, ages or occupations to appear more appealing have been widely reported, and safety organisations now routinely advise newcomers to meet unfamiliar matches only in public locations and to inform a friend of their plans in advance, treating each new connection with a degree of caution that traditional introductions rarely required.

## Paragraph 19

Paradoxically, having access to an almost limitless supply of potential partners does not appear to make the search for a relationship any easier, and some researchers argue it may even make it harder. Faced with an overwhelming array of choices, users often report a nagging sense that a better option might be only one swipe away, a mindset that can discourage genuine investment in any single connection and has been linked by some psychologists to rising rates of dissatisfaction and abrupt, unexplained withdrawal from budding relationships.

## Paragraph 20

The widespread adoption of these platforms has coincided with measurable shifts in how relationships begin, with a growing proportion of couples in several countries now reporting that they first met through an app or website rather than through friends, family or a shared workplace. Some sociologists view this shift as a natural evolution of courtship in an increasingly digital society, while others worry that it has subtly altered expectations around commitment, making it easier to abandon a relationship at the first sign of difficulty when an apparently endless supply of alternatives remains just a few taps away.

parts.title: The History of Guitars
parts.text:
The guitar's ancestry stretches back several thousand years to early stringed instruments found across a number of ancient civilisations, including simple lute-like instruments depicted in Egyptian and Mesopotamian artwork long before the modern instrument's recognisable shape had emerged. Scholars generally agree that the guitar's more immediate predecessors arrived in Europe through instruments such as the oud, brought to the Iberian Peninsula during centuries of Moorish rule, and later blended with local European instrument-making traditions. By the sixteenth century, a Spanish instrument called the vihuela, characterised by its curved waist and six paired strings, had become fashionable among the nobility, and many historians consider it the most direct forerunner of the guitar as it is understood today. Although similar stringed instruments existed independently elsewhere, it was this Iberian lineage that would eventually give rise to the shape and tuning conventions most closely associated with the modern guitar.

The instrument continued to evolve gradually over the following centuries, but it was the work of the Spanish luthier Antonio de Torres in the mid-nineteenth century that proved decisive in establishing what is now recognised as the classical guitar. Torres enlarged the body considerably beyond what earlier makers had considered standard, altered its proportions, and introduced a distinctive internal bracing pattern, arranged in a fan shape beneath the soundboard, that dramatically improved both volume and tonal richness. These innovations were not merely aesthetic; they addressed genuine acoustic limitations that had constrained the instrument's usefulness in larger performance settings. Torres's design proved so effective that virtually all classical guitars built since have followed his basic template closely, and contemporary luthiers still study his surviving instruments as a benchmark of craftsmanship, a testament to how thoroughly his approach came to define the instrument for generations that followed.

Meanwhile, in the United States, guitar-making developed along a somewhat different path, driven partly by the demands of folk, blues and country musicians who required an instrument capable of projecting over other performers in informal settings without amplification. Companies such as C. F. Martin and Company began producing steel-string acoustic guitars in the late nineteenth century, a departure from the gut strings traditionally used on classical instruments, producing a brighter, louder tone better suited to these emerging musical styles. Resonator guitars, which incorporated metal cones inside the body to mechanically amplify sound, appeared in the 1920s as an alternative solution to the same volume problem, becoming particularly associated with early blues musicians performing in noisy environments. As guitar manufacturing scaled up during this period, the instrument became considerably more affordable, placing it within reach of ordinary working musicians rather than remaining a costly item reserved largely for the wealthy or professionally trained.

The invention of the electric guitar in the following decades transformed the instrument's role in popular music more radically than any single development before it. Early experiments with electromagnetic pickups in the 1930s, including an unconventional lap-steel design nicknamed the Frying Pan for its distinctive round body, demonstrated that a guitar's vibrating strings could be converted into an electrical signal and amplified to previously unimaginable volumes. Manufacturers including Fender and Gibson subsequently refined this concept throughout the late 1940s and 1950s, releasing solid-body instruments such as the Telecaster, Stratocaster and Les Paul that would go on to define the sound of rock and roll and countless genres that followed. Because electric guitars no longer relied on a hollow, resonant body to project sound, builders gained far greater freedom over shape, weight and construction, enabling an era of rapid experimentation that produced many of the iconic instrument designs still manufactured, largely unchanged, today.

In the present day, guitar manufacturing spans an enormous range, from handcrafted instruments built individually by skilled luthiers commanding prices comparable to a car, to mass-produced models manufactured in large factories across Asia and sold at a fraction of that cost, putting a playable instrument within reach of beginners worldwide. Digital modelling technology now allows a single electric guitar, paired with modern amplifier software, to convincingly reproduce the tone of dozens of vintage instruments and amplifiers, a feat that would have seemed like science fiction to guitarists only a few decades earlier. Despite constant technological change surrounding it, the instrument's fundamental design, a resonant or electrically amplified body paired with a fretted neck and typically six strings, has remained remarkably stable since the innovations of Torres and the early electric pioneers, a rare case of a technology reaching a kind of settled maturity even as the music played on it continues to evolve in entirely new directions.

parts.title: Information Overload
parts.text:
Information overload refers to the difficulty a person experiences in comprehending an issue or making a decision when confronted with far more information than can reasonably be processed. Although the phenomenon predates modern technology, having been described by scholars as early as the 1970s in the context of an expanding print media landscape, it has intensified dramatically in the digital era, when a single smartphone can deliver a continuous stream of news alerts, messages and social media updates throughout every waking hour. Researchers estimate that many people now encounter a volume of information in a single day comparable to what earlier generations might have absorbed over the course of an entire month, raising questions about how the human brain, evolved for a far less data-saturated environment, can realistically cope with such a relentless influx.

Several converging factors have contributed to the current scale of the problem. The proliferation of internet-connected devices means most people now carry a source of near-infinite information in their pocket, while social media platforms are deliberately engineered to maximise engagement, often by delivering a constant stream of novel content calibrated to hold a user's attention for as long as possible. Round-the-clock news coverage adds a further layer of pressure, since major events are now reported, updated and re-reported within minutes rather than being consolidated into a single daily bulletin. Workplace communication tools compound the effect further still, with many employees now expected to monitor multiple messaging channels simultaneously throughout the working day, blurring what were once clearer boundaries between focused work and passive information consumption.

The cognitive consequences of this constant influx are increasingly well documented. Human working memory, the limited mental workspace used to hold and manipulate information over short periods, can only accommodate a small number of items at any one time, and repeatedly overloading it appears to degrade a person's ability to concentrate on any single task for an extended period. Some researchers describe a related phenomenon known as decision fatigue, in which the quality of a person's choices deteriorates measurably after making numerous smaller decisions earlier in the day, a pattern plausibly worsened by the sheer number of minor judgments, such as which notification to open first, that a typical smartphone user now makes without conscious reflection.

Beyond its effects on cognition, chronic exposure to excessive information has been linked to broader consequences for mental health and daily functioning. Surveys conducted in numerous countries have found associations between heavy social media use and elevated rates of self-reported anxiety, particularly among younger users who report feeling persistently behind on updates from their social circle. Sleep researchers have separately noted that late-night device use, driven partly by a reluctance to disconnect from an ongoing stream of information, disrupts the natural cycles that regulate healthy rest, with knock-on effects for concentration and mood the following day. Workplace productivity studies suggest a similar pattern, finding that employees interrupted frequently by notifications take considerably longer to return to a prior level of focus than commonly assumed.

In response, a range of strategies has emerged intended to help individuals manage their exposure to information more deliberately. Digital minimalism, an approach that encourages users to remove non-essential applications and consciously limit which sources of information they permit into their daily routine, has gained a considerable following among those seeking to reduce the sense of being perpetually overwhelmed. Simpler measures, such as disabling non-urgent notifications or setting specific times of day to check messages rather than responding immediately, have also proven effective in smaller studies, suggesting that even modest structural changes to how information is received can noticeably ease the burden without requiring users to withdraw from digital life entirely.

Looking ahead, some technologists argue that artificial intelligence may eventually help address the very problem that digital technology created, by filtering and summarising incoming information according to a user's genuine priorities rather than an algorithm's engagement targets. Sceptics counter that such systems introduce a fresh risk, since a curation tool that decides what a person does or does not see could just as easily narrow their exposure to a narrow set of perspectives or, if compromised, become a vector for misinformation delivered with the appearance of trustworthy personalisation. Whichever path institutions and individuals ultimately choose, most researchers agree that managing the balance between access to information and the human capacity to absorb it will remain a defining challenge of the coming decades.

parts.title: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out)
parts.text:
## Paragraph 15

The term itself is a relatively recent addition to everyday vocabulary, first appearing in academic marketing literature in the mid-1990s before spreading into mainstream use during the following decade. Early references described a general anxiety that one might be excluded from a rewarding social experience that others were currently enjoying, a feeling that, while not new to human psychology, had previously lacked a concise label. The abbreviation itself gained widespread recognition only after it began appearing regularly in magazine articles and online discussions around the early 2010s, roughly coinciding with the rapid growth of platforms that allowed people to broadcast their activities to wide networks of acquaintances in real time.

## Paragraph 16

Social media platforms are widely regarded as having intensified this feeling considerably beyond what earlier generations experienced. Where previous generations might have heard about a gathering secondhand, sometimes long after it had taken place, a constant stream of photographs, videos and status updates now allows people to witness events they were not invited to almost as they unfold. Researchers studying platform design have noted that features encouraging frequent checking, such as notifications and infinite scrolling feeds, appear specifically engineered to maximise the amount of time users spend monitoring the activities of others, a dynamic that some critics argue deliberately amplifies exactly the anxiety in question.

## Paragraph 17

At its psychological core, this phenomenon draws heavily on a long-established tendency to evaluate one's own circumstances by comparing them with those of other people. Seeing curated glimpses of an acquaintance's holiday, celebration or achievement can trigger an automatic, often unconscious assessment of one's own life as comparatively lacking, even when the comparison rests on an incomplete or deliberately flattering picture. Psychologists note that this kind of upward comparison, in which a person measures themselves against others who appear to be doing better, tends to produce more dissatisfaction than downward comparison, helping explain why carefully curated social media content proves particularly potent at triggering the feeling.

## Paragraph 18

Left unaddressed, this recurring sense of exclusion has been linked in several studies to broader difficulties with mental wellbeing, including elevated anxiety, lower self-esteem and, in some cases, symptoms resembling mild depression. Sleep researchers have separately observed that a reluctance to disengage from social platforms before bed, driven partly by a desire not to miss late-breaking updates, contributes to shorter and lower-quality sleep among frequent users, with knock-on effects for mood and concentration during the following day. Younger users, who often report checking social platforms most frequently, appear to be particularly susceptible to these compounding effects.

## Paragraph 19

Businesses and marketers have long understood the persuasive power of this particular anxiety and have built entire promotional strategies around it. Phrases emphasising scarcity or urgency, such as limited-time offers, exclusive early access or countdown timers displayed alongside a shrinking stock count, are deliberately designed to create the impression that failing to act immediately will result in a missed opportunity. Studies of consumer behaviour suggest that such tactics can measurably increase impulsive purchasing decisions, since the discomfort of potentially missing out frequently outweighs a more careful, considered evaluation of whether the purchase is actually necessary.

## Paragraph 20

Fortunately, a number of practical strategies have been shown to reduce the intensity of this feeling. Deliberately limiting the amount of time spent on social media, particularly during the evening, has been associated with improvements in both mood and sleep quality in several small-scale studies. Mental health professionals also recommend consciously practising gratitude for one's own circumstances rather than habitually comparing them with curated portrayals of other people's lives, alongside a reminder that most online content represents a carefully selected highlight rather than an accurate reflection of someone's everyday reality. Simply muting or unfollowing accounts that consistently trigger negative comparisons has also proven a straightforward and effective remedy for many users.

parts.title: The History of Rubber
parts.text:
Rubber's story begins not in a factory but in the tropical forests of Central and South America, where indigenous peoples had been extracting a milky sap from the Hevea tree and shaping it into balls, waterproof containers and crude footwear for centuries before Europeans ever encountered the material. Archaeological evidence indicates that the Olmec and Maya civilisations had been manufacturing rubber balls for ceremonial ballgames as early as 1600 BC, using latex collected from trees native to the region long before any European vessel reached the Americas. Early Spanish explorers who witnessed Mesoamerican ball games played with bouncing rubber spheres reportedly found the material's behaviour bizarre and slightly unsettling, since nothing resembling it existed anywhere in Europe at the time. Samples eventually made their way back across the Atlantic during the eighteenth century, where European scientists studied the curious substance with great curiosity but struggled initially to find any practical industrial application for it, since raw rubber in its untreated form presented serious drawbacks that limited its usefulness considerably.

Chief among these drawbacks was rubber's extreme sensitivity to temperature: in cold conditions it became stiff and brittle enough to crack, while in warm weather it turned soft, sticky and prone to melting into an unusable mess. Despite these limitations, the Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh found a commercially viable use for the material in the 1820s by sandwiching a layer of dissolved rubber between two pieces of fabric, creating a waterproof cloth that would eventually lend its inventor's name to raincoats sold under the Mackintosh brand. British and French armies later adopted rubberised fabric for military tents and equipment, recognising its practical value despite its imperfections, and demand for the material grew steadily even as manufacturers searched for a more reliable alternative. Although popular, these early garments still suffered from rubber's unreliable behaviour across seasons, becoming uncomfortably stiff in winter and unpleasantly tacky during summer, a problem that continued to frustrate manufacturers seeking a more dependable material.

The breakthrough that finally solved this problem arrived, according to popular accounts, largely by accident. In 1839, the American inventor Charles Goodyear reportedly spilled a mixture of rubber and sulfur onto a hot stove, discovering that the resulting material, once cooled, retained a springy, stable consistency across a far wider range of temperatures than untreated rubber ever had. Goodyear spent years refining this process, which became known as vulcanisation, before securing a patent, though he later became entangled in a lengthy and bitter legal dispute with the English inventor Thomas Hancock, who had independently developed a strikingly similar process and patented it in Britain only shortly after Goodyear's American filing. The process took its name from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire, a fitting reference given the intense heat required to transform raw rubber into its far more resilient vulcanised form, and manufacturers across Europe and North America adopted the technique within a matter of years. Vulcanised rubber proved dramatically more durable and reliable than anything that had come before it, and demand for the transformed material grew rapidly across numerous industries.

This surging demand triggered an economic boom throughout the Amazon basin during the final decades of the nineteenth century, as wild rubber trees native to the region suddenly became enormously valuable. Cities such as Manaus, deep within the Brazilian rainforest, grew extraordinarily wealthy almost overnight during this period, funding elaborate opera houses and grand boulevards financed entirely by the rubber trade, a prosperity that evaporated almost as quickly once the boom collapsed. The resulting rubber rush brought immense wealth to a small number of traders and plantation owners, but it also produced widespread and well-documented suffering, since much of the labour required to harvest wild rubber was extracted through coercive and often brutal practices imposed on indigenous communities, a pattern tragically mirrored in Belgian-controlled regions of central Africa during the same period. The Amazon's dominance of the global rubber trade collapsed abruptly in the early twentieth century after British botanists smuggled rubber tree seeds out of Brazil and successfully cultivated vast, far more efficient plantations in British colonies across Southeast Asia, permanently shifting the centre of world rubber production away from South America.

The next major transformation arrived during the Second World War, when wartime disruptions to Southeast Asian supply routes created a severe shortage of natural rubber for Allied nations, spurring an intensive research effort into synthetic alternatives manufactured from petroleum-based chemicals rather than tree sap. Scientists in the United States and Germany developed viable synthetic rubber compounds under considerable wartime pressure, and by the war's end, synthetic materials had become firmly established alongside natural rubber as a reliable industrial staple. Among the most successful synthetic formulations to emerge from this period was styrene-butadiene rubber, which remains one of the most widely produced synthetic rubbers in the world today and is used extensively in the manufacture of vehicle tyres. Today, both natural and synthetic rubber remain indispensable to modern life, appearing in products ranging from vehicle tyres and industrial seals to medical gloves and footwear, a lasting testament to a material first discovered by people living thousands of years before the modern industries it now underpins were ever imagined.
